extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetry, drama, aesthetics, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles for composing and judging poetic drama (tragedy and comedy) as discussed through an Aristotelian/classical-aesthetic lens. Emphasis on how universalisation, idealisation, character-drawing, and modes of humour function in poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation by suppression of accidental features
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject matter of artistic representation already possesses grandeur or beauty, its dominant characteristics will be made more prominent by the suppression of accidental features, and the ideal form that results will have added elements of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Eliminate non-essential, incidental details to reveal a higher beauty; example: a portrait reproduces likeness yet is idealised. Anti-patterns: literal, cluttered representation that leaves accidental features uncurbed and thus weakens the ideal form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation does not imply flawless virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Idealised portraiture does not consist in presenting characters of flawless virtue; the tragic hero may have faults but retain a moral nobility that warrants ideal status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Retain some faults to preserve human truth (e.g., Achilles has defects yet moral nobility). Scoring note: idealisation should heighten commanding faculties without disturbing the equilibrio of character that makes a typical human being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain equipoise of character when emphasizing qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some particular quality or group of qualities must be thrown into relief; some commanding faculty heightened, provided that in so doing the equipoise of character, which constitutes a typical human being, is not disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: When accentuating traits, ensure the character still reads as a plausible whole; avoid exaggerations that destroy internal balance. Example: emphasize nobility while keeping other human faculties proportionate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: universalise through the individual (idealised persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy combines universalisation and embellishment; it manifests the type through the individual, combining the individual and the universal into a harmonious representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Create characters who are individual and fully particular yet embody universal human truths; scoring: highest tragedy achieves both individual depth and universal resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: focus on follies and the laughable, not moral perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy concerns itself with the follies and foibles, the flaws and imperfections of mankind; it exhibits evil not as it is in its essential nature, but as a thing to be laughed at rather than hated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Use comic treatment to expose ordinary human inconsistencies; avoid treating comic figures as morally exemplary. Anti-patterns: treating comic characters as tragic exemplars or attempting to moralize their foibles into heroic traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic judgment on which imperfections to depict
rubrics_metrics.description: At what precise point imperfections are to be regarded as accidental, abnormal, irregular, or as presenting so marked a deviation from the type as to be unworthy of lasting embodiment in art is a problem whose answer will vary with history and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Decide case-by-case which defects belong to universal human nature and which should be excluded; be aware this varies by period and art form. Scoring note: successful works make historically and artistically defensible choices about included imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ‘ugly’ or flawed elements to contribute to overall beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual character, though ugly when abstracted, may contribute to the beauty of the whole when universalised or shown as nugatory and ridiculous within the comedy's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Contextualize flaws so that they function as parts of a larger aesthetically pleasing structure; anti-pattern: isolating flaws without integrating them into the overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ludicrous = defect/ugliness that is not painful or destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive; the comic mask is ugly and distorted but does not imply pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Aim for incongruity that provokes laughter without harming the subject; avoid cruelty or genuinely harmful portrayals. Distinction: exclude malice from the pure ludicrous; malice may season a joke but is not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity must involve a transition (surprise) to be ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity, in order to be ludicrous, requires a transition—a change of mood—resulting in the discovery either of an unexpected resemblance where there was unlikeness, or of an unexpected unlikeness where there was resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Structure moments so that surprise or a mood-shift reveals the incongruity; the comedic pleasure arises from the shock of painless incongruity. Anti-pattern: static incongruity without a revealing transition tends not to be genuinely ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy generalises by typification (names/titles indicating type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often discards historical names and adopts names which suggest characteristic qualities; names/titles can immediately signal the type (e.g., the Boor, the Parasite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Use expressive, emblematic naming to prompt instant recognition of a type; example: Middle/New Comedy titles and character names that connote occupations/traits. Anti-pattern: arbitrary or incongruous naming that undermines type-recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comedy proper from personal satire/invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy proper is a representation of the universal; personal satire or invective represents the particular (e.g., old political comedy aimed at individuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: For genuine comedy, avoid coarse personal abuse and caricature aimed solely at specific persons; instead aim for type-based, general critique. Example: Aristotle excludes lampooners who employed coarse abusive language from 'genuine' comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure realism (literal prosaic imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure realism—the literal and prosaic imitation which reaches perfection in a jugglery of the senses by which the copy is mistaken for the original—is forbidden in the Greek aesthetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Eschew slavish mimicry that substitutes sensory trickery for poetic truth. Anti-pattern: works that prioritize surface illusion over structural, thematic or universal truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely fantastical or symbolic hybrids that violate nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure symbolism—fantastic shapes (lion body with human head, etc.)—that create impossible compounds and violate nature's laws is forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Symbolism must remain intelligible and consistent with poetic truth; avoid allegorical hybrids that are incoherent or fail to correspond with perceivable ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate irrational/fantastical elements coherently to maintain plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements (magic, transformations) are acceptable provided they function as accessories that do not disturb the main impression; presented with vividness and coherence the impossible becomes plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: When using fantastical devices, keep them coherent within the work's internal logic so the fiction looks like truth (Odyssey as example). Anti-pattern: inserting magic/absurdity that breaks the reader's sense of poetic plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek aesthetic: reasonableness, measure, and self-restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek imagination is under strict control of reason, limited by a sense of measure and a faculty of self-restraint; it employs a reserve of power and temperate strength without ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Prefer harmony, restraint, clarity over dazzling excess; the poet should 'see truly' and express harmoniously. Scoring: works demonstrating measured restraint and intelligible composition are favoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate non-essential attributes to create clear, intelligible types (myth/god formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In assigning spheres and duties, all that is non-essential is eliminated so that mythic figures become clear, calm, and intelligible—attributes common to other gods fall out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Simplify composites by removing redundant attributes to produce a vivid, unified type; anti-pattern: cluttered mythic figures full of overlapping, unnecessary attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy tends to isolate and exaggerate a dominant characteristic (risk of caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy, looking at a single aspect of life, often embodies a dominant characteristic or leading passion so that the single attribute becomes the man; this abstraction almost of necessity runs to caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Be aware that isolating one trait produces distinctive comic effect but risks flattening character; balance specificity with enough other features to avoid total caricature if deeper portrayal is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour enriched by sympathy merges comic and tragic insights
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern humour, enriched by sympathy, interpenetrates tragedy and comedy: humour looks below the surface, rediscovers hidden incongruities, and finds material for both laughter and tears—humour is the meeting-point of tragedy and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Use sympathetic observation to deepen comic effect and enable universalising power (e.g., Don Quixote). Scoring: humour that balances affection and insight attains broader universality than mere satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at universality via generalisation from concrete facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's method: start from concrete facts and generalise—poetry aims to express the universal by disengaging and formulating universal elements from observed literature and life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides: Build from observed particulars but abstract to universal laws or types; successful poetic theory or practice generalises without losing grounding in concrete detail.
